records.sourceFile: Transdermal Uptake of Substances Banned in Sports and Its Relevance for Doping Controls - 2025.pdf

paper.citation: Krombholz S, Korsmeier L, Thevis M. Transdermal uptake of substances banned in sports and its relevance for doping controls. International Journal of Sports Medicine. 2025.
paper.abstract: This narrative review explores the implications of transdermal uptake of substances banned in sports for doping control analysis. It covers skin absorption, transdermal forms of WADA-listed substances, and cases in which athletes were exposed to banned substances through the skin.
paper.tldr: Several banned substances, especially clostebol and anabolic steroids, can pass through the skin and be detected in urine for days to weeks. Athletes and teams should avoid sharing topical products and should check any cream or patch against the Prohibited List before use.
paper.methods: Narrative review. The authors searched PubMed and Google Scholar using MeSH and free-text terms for doping and skin or transdermal routes, combined with individual WADA-listed substances, and screened titles, abstracts and full texts. Human studies were prioritised over animal or in vitro work. No pooled analysis was performed.
paper.findings: The authors report that transdermal testosterone and other anabolic agents are absorbed, and that controlled applications of clostebol, DHCMT, metandienone and oxandrolone gave detectable urinary metabolites, in one study for up to 14 days. A 5 mg clostebol cream applied with only transient contact was detectable as the M1 metabolite. Unpublished data from the authors' laboratory showed that as little as 10 micrograms of the SARMs LGD-4033 and S-23 applied to the forearm was detectable in urine for up to 13 and 16 days, respectively. Transdermal capromorelin was detectable in urine for at least 48 hours in three volunteers. Transdermal routes can change metabolite patterns and ratios compared with oral dosing, but the authors say these differences vary between individuals and need larger studies.
paper.limitations: Many cited studies use animal or in vitro skin models, the human studies are small, and the SARM detection data are unpublished. Articles were appraised for relevance and quality, but no pooled analysis or formal risk-of-bias results are reported. The authors note that interindividual variability in skin condition, age and site of application makes general conclusions difficult.
paper.practicalImplications: Treat topical products as a possible route of exposure. Check creams, gels and patches that athletes or staff use or share against the Prohibited List, and be aware that clostebol creams used for minor skin injuries were the product most often cited by athletes who attributed a positive test to skin contact with others.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: this review does not assess performance effects. Its relevance is to doping risk: athletes and staff should avoid unnecessary exposure to banned topical products, because even brief contact can produce an adverse analytical finding.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: this review cannot inform return-to-sport or rehabilitation decisions. Its only relevance to injured athletes is that topical clostebol products used for skin injuries can cause a positive test, so check any topical treatment against the Prohibited List before use.

records.sourceFile: Treatment of pectoralis major tendon tears - A systematic review and meta-analysis of operative and nonoperative treatment.pdf

paper.citation: Bodendorfer BM, McCormick BP, Wang DX, Looney AM, Conroy CM, Fryar CM, et al. Treatment of pectoralis major tendon tears: a systematic review and meta-analysis of operative and nonoperative treatment. Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine. 2020;8(2):2325967119900813.
paper.abstract: A PRISMA systematic review and meta-analysis of 23 operative studies and nonoperative outcomes for pectoralis major tendon tears, scored with the MINORS tool, compared functional, strength, cosmesis and deformity outcomes between treatment groups.
paper.tldr: Surgical repair of pectoralis major tendon tears gave better strength, function and appearance than nonoperative care in pooled data, with a 14% complication rate. The nonoperative evidence is thin, so treat the comparison as a guide rather than a definitive answer.
paper.methods: PRISMA systematic review of six databases (to February 2019) with random-effects meta-analysis of English-language studies with at least 6 months of follow-up and 5 cases. Study quality was assessed with MINORS. Continuous outcomes were pooled with mixed models and proportions with Freeman-Tukey transformation.
paper.findings: Operative repair was associated with higher functional outcome scores (3.66 vs 2.96, P=.027), full isometric strength in 97.5% vs 20.4% (P<.001), smaller isokinetic strength loss (-8.6% vs -37.5%, P<.001), less resting deformity (1.2% vs 100%, P<.001) and higher cosmesis satisfaction (91.6% vs 77.8%, P=.037), per Table 4. Range of motion did not differ (P=.862). The pooled operative complication rate was 14.21%, including rerupture 3.08%, persistent pain 3.03% and additional surgery 2.28%.
paper.limitations: The nonoperative group had 61 tears and a mean follow-up of 13.45 months, against 41.43 months for operative patients. Most studies were of lower quality (one level 2, four level 3 and 18 level 4), and the population ranged from professional to recreational athletes. The abstract and Results disagree on which figures belong to resting deformity (98.85%) and cosmesis satisfaction (13.79%); Table 4 supports the abstract's labels, so the table values are reported here. Sport-specific return to play could not be analysed.
paper.practicalImplications: For a complete pectoralis major rupture in an athlete who needs full strength and appearance, the pooled data favour surgical repair, with an expectation of roughly one in seven patients having a complication. Discuss the rerupture and persistent pain risk with the patient, and remember that the nonoperative data are limited.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: this review shows that operatively repaired athletes regained more isometric and isokinetic strength than nonoperatively managed patients, which matters for pressing and pulling performance. It does not report sport-specific return or bench press outcomes for the nonoperative group, so the strength gap cannot be quantified for athletes.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: the review supports surgical repair when a return to high-level strength work is required, and it reports a return to preinjury activity of about 95% after repair. It does not report return-to-sport timelines or sport-specific criteria, so use it as a guide for the surgical decision, not as a clearance standard.

records.sourceFile: Trends in match injury risk in professional male rugby union - A 16-season review the Professional Rugby Injury Surveillance Project.pdf

paper.citation: West SW, Starling L, Kemp S, Williams S, Cross M, Taylor A, et al. Trends in match injury risk in professional male rugby union: a 16-season review of 10 851 match injuries in the English Premiership (2002-2019): the Professional Rugby Injury Surveillance Project. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2020.
paper.abstract: Match injuries in English Premiership rugby were recorded across 16 seasons from 2002/2003 to 2018/2019 in the Professional Rugby Injury Surveillance Project. The study describes incidence, severity, burden and concussion trends over that period.
paper.tldr: Across 16 seasons of English Premiership rugby, injury incidence stayed flat, but injuries got more severe and concussion rose sharply. Concussion and tackle-related injuries deserve priority in prevention and in return-to-play planning.
paper.methods: Prospective surveillance of men's Premiership, National Cup and European Cup matches. Clubs recorded time-loss injuries (more than 24 hours) and exposure, and injuries were checked against match officials' report cards from 2016/17. Incidence, severity and burden were calculated per season and trends tested with linear regression and false discovery rate correction.
paper.findings: Incidence was stable at 87 per 1000 hours (95% CI 82 to 92), with a mean severity of 25 days and a burden of 2,178 days per 1000 hours. Mean severity (beta 1.2 days per year) and burden rose over time. Concussion incidence (beta 1.2 per 1000 hours per year), severity and burden rose, and concussion was the most common injury from 2011. The tackle caused 43% of injuries, and the knee had the highest burden (493 days per 1000 hours). Running-related injury incidence fell.
paper.limitations: The authors note that small systematic changes in the method occurred over the period and that the system moved from paper to web recording in 2012. Causes of rising severity could not be determined from surveillance data. The abstract dates the concussion rise from 2009/2010, while the Results give 2011/2012 for incidence and burden, so the start date should be read from the Results.
paper.practicalImplications: Expect a match injury to cost a mean of about 25 days, although the median is 9 days and 43% of players return within 7 days, because a few long injuries raise the mean. Plan the tackle, knee, ankle and shoulder injury risk alongside concussion prevention, and use the published burden figures as benchmarks for return-to-play planning within the club.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: this surveillance shows the tackle is the highest-burden match event and that knee, ankle and shoulder injuries carry the highest burden, which informs where to focus injury prevention for professional players. It does not test any intervention, so it cannot show that a specific training change would reduce injury.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: the authors describe expected injury severities by body region and injury type that can guide club return-to-play planning. The study gives population averages only, and it does not set return criteria or confirm that longer stand-downs reduce re-injury.

records.sourceFile: Triceps Ruptures After        Fluoroquinolone Antibiotics- A Report of 2 Cases.pdf

paper.citation: Shybut TB, Puckett ER. Triceps ruptures after fluoroquinolone antibiotics: a report of 2 cases. Sports Health. 2017.
paper.abstract: The authors describe two patients who ruptured the triceps brachii tendon in the months after treatment with fluoroquinolone antibiotics, a link not previously reported for triceps. Both were repaired surgically with good outcomes, and the authors advise that the risk be considered when choosing antibiotics for athletes.
paper.tldr: Two patients ruptured a triceps tendon about three months after fluoroquinolone treatment and recovered well after surgical repair. Consider a non-fluoroquinolone antibiotic for athletes where there is a choice, though the link is unproven.
paper.methods: Case report of two patients, with clinical examination, imaging (radiograph and MRI), surgical repair and rehabilitation described. No histology was available.
paper.findings: Case 1 (60-year-old man) had a complete triceps avulsion with retraction 3 months after levofloxacin and was repaired with a modified double-row suture anchor technique. Case 2 (47-year-old judoka) had a full-thickness tear with 7 mm retraction; he was injured 1 month before presentation and had taken ciprofloxacin 'three months prior', and he was repaired with a transosseous technique. Both were rehabilitated. Case 1 returned to golf at 5 months and was fully recovered at 14 months. Case 2 had a healed repair at 8 months and returned to randori and coaching, but not open competition, at 10 months.
paper.limitations: The authors state that the extent of fluoroquinolone contribution cannot be determined, that histology was not available, and that firm prescribing guidelines for athletes are lacking. Both patients were men with a single exposure history, and the case 1 patient was not described as an athlete.
paper.practicalImplications: When treating an athlete, consider whether a non-fluoroquinolone antibiotic is a suitable alternative, and ask about recent fluoroquinolone use when assessing an unexplained tendon injury. Consider this risk before fluoroquinolone use around tendon repair surgery, as the authors suggest.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: this report does not address training or performance. Its relevance is to medication decisions for athletes, since a tendon rupture could remove an athlete from training for months.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: the report describes repair and rehabilitation with return to golf at 5 months and to judo training without competition at 10 months. These are two individual cases with no return-to-play criteria, so the report cannot be used to set a return timeline for a triceps repair.

records.sourceFile: Two Genetic Loci associated with        Medial Collateral Ligament Injury.pdf

paper.citation: Roos AK, Avins AL, Ahmed MA, Kleimeyer JP, Roos TR, Fredericson M, et al. Two Genetic Loci Associated with Medial Collateral Ligament Injury. Int J Sports Med. 2017;38:501-507.
paper.abstract: Genome-wide association study of MCL injury in 1,572 cases and 100,931 controls from a Kaiser Permanente cohort. Two loci reached genome-wide significance (rs80351309 and rs6083471) with moderate effects, and the authors call for replication in athletes.
paper.tldr: Two genetic variants, one of them rare, were associated with MCL injury in a large general adult cohort. They are not yet usable for identifying at-risk athletes, because they need replication and have no known functional mechanism.
paper.methods: Genome-wide association analysis of RPGEH/GERA genotype data with imputation to a 1000 Genomes reference, logistic regression adjusted for sex, age, ancestry principal components and genotyping batch, and fixed-effects meta-analysis across four ancestry groups. Cases were identified from ICD-9 codes in the electronic health record.
paper.findings: Two SNPs passed genome-wide significance: rs80351309 (OR 2.12, P=6.8 x 10^-9, imputation R2 0.56) and rs6083471 (OR 1.57, P=6.3 x 10^-9, R2 0.97). The European group gave the smallest P values for both, and the odds ratios were in the same direction across groups. Neither SNP lies in a coding region or has a known expression effect.
paper.limitations: Diagnoses come from ICD-9 codes, which may be inaccurate and cannot separate injury grades. Sport participation was not recorded, so the authors cannot tell whether the signal comes mainly from people active in sport. The Latin American, African American and East Asian groups had few cases, and rs80351309 was imputed with moderate accuracy.
paper.practicalImplications: These results do not support using either SNP to identify athletes at risk of MCL injury. Replication in independent cohorts, ideally including athletes, is needed before any screening use.
paper.athleteDev: Not applicable yet: the markers have not been tested in athletes and should not be used for talent or risk screening.
paper.rtp: The study addresses MCL injury occurrence, not recovery or return to sport, so it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions.

records.sourceFile: Two or four weeks acute-chronic workload ratio is more useful to prevent injuries in soccer.pdf

paper.citation: Fousekis A, Fousekis K, Fousekis G, Vaitsis N, Terzidis I, Christoulas K, et al. Two or Four Weeks Acute: Chronic Workload Ratio Is More Useful to Prevent Injuries in Soccer? Appl Sci. 2023;13:495.
paper.abstract: GPS-measured external load in 35 professional soccer players over one season was compared between nine players with non-contact injuries and matched non-injured players. Acute:chronic workload ratios over four- and two-week windows before injury were higher in injured players, and the two-week model separated the groups on all six load variables.
paper.tldr: In this small season-long GPS study, injured soccer players showed higher short-term load spikes before non-contact injury, and the two-week window separated them more consistently than the four-week window. Use it to watch for load spikes, not as a validated injury threshold.
paper.methods: Thirty-five Greek professional players wore GPS vests across one season. ACWR was calculated for total distance, speed bands, accelerations and decelerations as the load in the injury week divided by the average of the previous four or two weeks. Injured players were compared with matched non-injured players using Wilcoxon tests.
paper.findings: Nine players had non-contact injuries (4.5 per 1000 h). Injured players exceeded the ACWR 1.3 limit several times and non-injured players never did. Three of six variables differed in the four-week model and all six in the two-week model; distance above 25 km/h had the highest injured-player mean ACWR (1.58 and 1.47) but was not significant in the four-week model (p=0.085).
paper.limitations: Nine injuries and a small matched sample limit power. The methods report N=18 for the statistics against 35 players, and the authors note that match participation time was not identical across players.
paper.practicalImplications: Compare each player's load in the current week with the average of the previous two weeks, as well as the previous four, with particular attention to high-speed running and acceleration volume. Treat values above 1.3 as a prompt to review the week rather than as a settled cut-off.
paper.athleteDev: The authors suggest the two-week ACWR, particularly for high-speed running and acceleration volume, as a more sensitive early warning when planning individual microcycle loads.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It concerns the lead-up to non-contact injury in players who were not yet injured.

records.sourceFile: Ultrasound as a predictor of time-loss injury for the patellar tendon, Achilles tendon and plantar fascia in collegiate athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Cushman DM, Stokes D, Vu L, Corcoran B, Fredericson M, Eby SF, et al. Ultrasound as a predictor of time-loss injury for the patellar tendon, Achilles tendon and plantar fascia in division I collegiate athletes. Br J Sports Med. 2025;59:1-8.
paper.abstract: Prospective observational study of 695 athlete scans (538 distinct NCAA Division I athletes) from three institutions who had preseason ultrasound of the patellar tendon, Achilles tendon and plantar fascia and were followed for time-loss injury over the next year. Preseason sonographic abnormalities were associated with time-loss injury in all three structures.
paper.tldr: A preseason ultrasound abnormality in the patellar tendon, Achilles tendon or plantar fascia was linked to a much higher chance of time-loss injury in that structure, more strongly than prior injury or pain at the scan. A normal scan was rarely followed by injury, but most abnormal scans were not followed by injury.
paper.methods: Preseason ultrasound video captures of both patellar tendons, Achilles tendons and plantar fasciae were reviewed blind to athlete identity. Injuries were recorded by athletic training staff and physicians over the following year. Adjusted relative risks came from generalised linear models (adjusting for prior injury and pain at the scan), with Cox models for time to injury and sensitivity, specificity and predictive values for screening.
paper.findings: Abnormalities were found in 36.6% of patellar tendons, 7.5% of Achilles tendons and 2.8% of plantar fasciae. Adjusted RR of time-loss injury was 8.9 (95% CI 3.7-21.4) for patellar tendon, 18.8 (7.2-48.8) for Achilles and 21.0 (6.4-68.1) for plantar fascia, all P<0.001. Ultrasound sensitivity was higher than that of prior injury or pain for all three structures.
paper.limitations: Sample count conflict: the abstract and Table 1 read as 695 athletes, but the Results section shows 695 scans from 538 distinct athletes (403 scanned once, 113 twice, 22 three times), analysed with a cluster-robust model per athlete per season. Few injuries (44 patellar, 22 Achilles, 9 plantar fascia) gave wide confidence intervals. Findings were recorded only as present or absent, self-reported pain was used, and clinical injury diagnosis had no gold standard. The study covers collegiate athletes and the authors caution against applying it to adolescents or older athletes.
paper.practicalImplications: A preseason ultrasound check of the patellar tendon, Achilles tendon and plantar fascia may help identify athletes to monitor more closely. Pair it with workload and neuromuscular, strength and range-of-motion assessment rather than using it alone.
paper.athleteDev: Use an abnormal preseason tendon or fascia scan to flag an athlete for closer workload and neuromuscular review, not as a stand-alone reason to restrict training.
paper.rtp: This study concerns preseason injury risk, with structures that had prior rupture or surgery excluded, not return to sport after injury. It cannot be used to decide when an injured athlete is ready to return.

records.sourceFile: Ultrasound shear wave seeds reduced following hamstring strain injury but not after returning to sport.pdf

paper.citation: Crawford SK, Wille CM, Joachim MR, Lee KS, Heiderscheit BC. Ultrasound shear wave seeds reduced following hamstring strain injury but not after returning to sport. Insights Imaging. 2024;15:7.
paper.abstract: Compared ultrasound shear wave speed (SWS) between injured and uninjured hamstrings in collegiate athletes with hamstring strain injury at time of injury, at return to sport and 12 weeks after return. SWS was lower in the injured limb only at time of injury.
paper.tldr: Shear wave speed was lower in the injured hamstring at time of injury but matched the uninjured limb at return to sport and 12 weeks later. It may add a muscle stiffness measure to imaging, but it is not a return-to-sport test.
paper.methods: Observational prospective study, analysed cross-sectionally, of collegiate athletes with MRI-confirmed hamstring strain. SWS was measured with a clinical ultrasound system at the injury site and matched site on the uninjured limb, averaging three 5 mm regions per muscle. A linear mixed-effects model tested the limb by time-point interaction.
paper.findings: Among 15 athletes (16 injuries), injured-limb SWS was 1.82 m/s vs 2.05 m/s uninjured at time of injury (difference 0.23 m/s, 95% CI 0.05-0.41, P=0.006). At return to sport (0.15 m/s, P=0.23) and 12 weeks after (-0.11 m/s, P=0.84) there was no difference. The limb by time-point interaction was significant (P=0.02).
paper.limitations: Small sample at each time point, with the 12-week group smallest. Only injuries with MRI oedema were included, and time to return to sport varied from 19 to 49 days. The cross-sectional design cannot follow healing within individuals.
paper.practicalImplications: SWS at the injury site could be considered alongside ultrasound or MRI at the time of injury. Its value for return-to-sport decisions has not been shown, so clinical criteria should remain the main basis.
paper.athleteDev: Clinicians could record SWS at the injury site as an extra measure of muscle stiffness at injury, but it is not yet a performance or readiness metric.
paper.rtp: The study found no average between-limb difference at return to sport in a small sample, but it did not link SWS to readiness or re-injury. SWS cannot yet be used as a return-to-sport criterion.

records.sourceFile: Use of publicly obtained data in sports medicine research - A systematic review and bibliometric analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Inclan PM, Kuhn AW, Troyer SC, Solomon GS, Matava MJ. Use of Publicly Obtained Data in Sports Medicine Research: A Systematic Review and Bibliometric Analysis. Am J Sports Med. 2023.
paper.abstract: The authors systematically reviewed 209 sports medicine studies (2000 to 2022) that relied solely on publicly obtained data about collegiate, semiprofessional and professional athletes. They found rapid growth in these studies, wide variation in injuries and data sources, and frequent weak methods reporting.
paper.tldr: Studies built only from news reports and team websites are now common in sports medicine, but their sources and methods are often vague. Read their injury and return-to-play findings with that in mind.
paper.methods: The authors followed PRISMA and searched Ovid MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science and CINAHL in February 2022 for studies from 2000 onward. Two reviewers screened and extracted data, and the review summarised bibliometric and study characteristics descriptively; no formal bias assessment was done, although MINORS methodological scores were reported.
paper.findings: Of 209 included studies, 173 (82.8%) were published after 2016. Most covered North American professional leagues, led by the NFL (28.4%), MLB (23.0%), NBA (15.2%) and NHL (13.6%). Concussion (21.1%), ACL (16.2%) and ulnar collateral ligament injuries (11.3%) were the most common topics. Of the studies, 25.4% used one data source, 31.1% named nonspecific sources or only cited prior literature, and one reported no source.
paper.limitations: Nearly all included studies were retrospective and lacked a sample size estimate (the text says all were retrospective, but Table 1 lists 2 prospective cohorts), and the review did not assess how complete or accurate each study's injury capture was. The authors also note that defining POD methodology was difficult, because select studies combined public data with video analysis or a surveillance data set, although most relied entirely on public data.
paper.practicalImplications: When reading a public-data injury study, check the number and specificity of its sources, whether the search was reproducible, and the time period it covers. Treat headline incidence or return-to-play numbers from such studies as provisional.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: Public-data studies of player performance after injury are common, but the review shows their sources and time frames vary widely. Use them to generate questions, and check them against league or internal data before using them in athlete evaluation.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: Many included studies report return-to-play rates from news reports, and the authors warn that these may miss less severe injuries and over-represent high-profile athletes. The review does not establish valid return-to-play rates, so it should not be used as a basis for return-to-play decisions.

records.sourceFile: Use of the heat tolerance test to assess recovery from exertional heat stroke.pdf

paper.citation: Mitchell KM, Cheuvront SN, King MA, Mayer TA, Leon LR, Kenefick RW. Use of the heat tolerance test to assess recovery from exertional heat stroke. Temperature. 2019;6(2):106-119.
paper.abstract: The authors review exertional heat stroke (EHS) and the return-to-activity decision, focusing on the heat tolerance test (HTT). They conclude that the HTT has limited sensitivity and little or no specificity for recovery, and that its criteria and follow-up data are inadequate.
paper.tldr: The heat tolerance test is used to help decide when people can return after exertional heat stroke, but it has not been shown to predict recovery or recurrence. Use it as one input alongside clinical markers and gradual return, not as a stand-alone clearance test.
paper.methods: This is a narrative review with no described literature search. The authors summarise heat-balance physiology, blood biomarkers, return-to-activity guidance and the HTT protocols (including the Israeli Defense Force versions and tolerance criteria), and they describe the test's limitations and knowledge gaps.
paper.findings: The review describes several HTT protocols and criteria that have changed over time, and reports that blood biomarkers can return to baseline while residual organ damage may persist. It cites that only 10% of people fail the IDF HTT on the first attempt and that less than 2% fail on retest three months later, but the authors note that no follow-up data show the test predicts recurrence. Women were more often classified as heat intolerant, mainly because of heart rate, and the test may not suit endurance athletes or higher workloads.
paper.limitations: The authors state that there is no experimentally validated evidence that the HTT predicts recurrence, and that follow-up data on people who passed it are lacking. Much of the evidence is from military samples and non-human models, and the review is not systematic.
paper.practicalImplications: Do not use a single HTT result as clearance to return after exertional heat stroke. Use it alongside normal clinical blood work, physician review, and gradual return with heat acclimatisation, and record follow-up outcomes so the test's value can be judged.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: Heat acclimatisation and fitness affect heat tolerance, so return-to-training plans after heat illness should build load gradually and in the heat. The review does not give validated training prescriptions, and the HTT does not match high-workload or endurance demands.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: The review supports an individualised, staged return after EHS, with physician judgement and normal blood markers, and it does not endorse the HTT as a sole return-to-play test. It cannot establish safe timelines or a validated pass criterion for return to play.

records.sourceFile: Validity of research based on public data in sports medicine - A quantitative assessment of anterior cruciate ligament injuries in the NFL.pdf

paper.citation: Inclan PM, Chang PS, Mack CD, Solomon GS, Brophy RH, Hinton RY, et al. Validity of Research Based on Public Data in Sports Medicine: A Quantitative Assessment of Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injuries in the National Football League. Am J Sports Med. 2021.
paper.abstract: Systematic review of publicly obtained data studies of NFL injuries (42 studies, 14 on ACL injuries), with ACL injuries compared against the NFL Injury Surveillance System. Public-data studies captured a mean of 66% of ACL injuries, with capture varying by position and lowest on special teams. The authors conclude that these studies underreport injury incidence and favour more popular players.
paper.tldr: Public-data NFL injury studies missed about a third of the ACL injuries teams reported to the league, with the largest gaps for linemen and special teams. Injury counts from public sources should be read as undercounts that favour popular players.
paper.methods: PRISMA systematic review of English-language original research and grey literature on NFL injuries from public sources, searched in June 2019 across Medline, Embase, Scopus and ClinicalTrials.gov. Two reviewers screened records. For the ACL studies with usable post-2000 data, the capture rate was the study's ACL injury count divided by the NFL surveillance count for the same period, with three studies from one group analysed as a single dataset.
paper.findings: Of 42 POD studies, 35 (83%) were published in 2015 or later. The five ACL comparisons captured a mean of 66% of ACL injuries (range 31% to 90%). In three studies with position data, capture averaged 86% for skill players, 72% for midskill players, 61% for linemen and 35% for special teams injuries, and the authors conclude the studies favour injuries in more popular players.
paper.limitations: Comparison was limited to what the published studies reported, so player-level detail could not be checked. Some studies grouped positions, which affects position-level rates. Two authors list NFL affiliations, one lists IQVIA, several disclose NFL consulting fees, and one is chair of the NFL Research and Innovation Committee.
paper.practicalImplications: Treat injury counts drawn only from public media, fantasy sites or team reports as incomplete, especially for linemen and special teams. Use a standardised surveillance source when estimating incidence.
paper.athleteDev: Do not use public-report injury counts to benchmark players or compare positions, because these sources miss injuries unevenly across positions.
paper.rtp: The review addresses how injuries are counted, not how athletes recover, so it does not provide return-to-play outcomes or rates that staff can apply to an individual athlete.

records.sourceFile: Velocity specific time and       dependent adaptations following a standardized Nordic hamstring   exercise     training.pdf

paper.citation: Alt T, Nodler YT, Severin J, Knicker AJ, Strüder HK. Velocity-specific and time-dependent adaptations following a standardized Nordic Hamstring Exercise training. Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2017.
paper.abstract: The study examined the effects of a standardised 4-week NHE programme on thigh strength and muscle balance in 16 male sprinters, using kinetic and kinematic monitoring and isokinetic tests. Eccentric hamstring strength increased by 6-14%, with significant increases in peak and mean moments throughout training. The biggest adaptations appeared at the highest test velocity two weeks after training ended.
paper.tldr: A four-week NHE programme improved eccentric hamstring strength and hamstring-to-quad balance in sprinters, with the largest gains showing up two weeks after the last session. The study does not show that it reduces injuries.
paper.methods: Within-subject repeated-measures design with 16 male sprinters (mean age 21.6 years), using a 4-week regular-training baseline period as each athlete's own control. Participants completed 12 NHE sessions over four weeks on a dynamometer, six rope-assisted and six unassisted, targeting a constant knee extension velocity of about 15 degrees per second. Kinetic and kinematic NHE data were recorded during selected sessions, and isokinetic knee flexor and extensor tests were run at baseline, before training and three times over the 2 weeks after training.
paper.findings: Peak and mean eccentric moments of unassisted repetitions rose significantly across training (P < 0.001). Eccentric hamstring strength increased by 6-14%, with the largest gains at the highest test velocity (150 degrees per second, +14.3%) two weeks after training. Concentric hamstring peak moments rose by 5.6% at 30 degrees per second and 7.7% at 150 degrees per second between baseline and post-3 testing, functional H:Q ratio improved by 12-14%, and quadriceps measures did not change.
paper.limitations: There was no separate control group, the sample was heterogeneous in training history and level, and only one device and one short, low-volume protocol were studied, with no injury or sprint outcomes. Kinetics were measured bilaterally, so the contribution of each leg is unknown.
paper.practicalImplications: A four-week NHE block can raise eccentric hamstring strength and improve hamstring-to-quadriceps balance in sprinters. The biggest high-velocity strength change appeared two weeks after the programme ended, during regular training, so testing immediately after a block may understate the gain.
paper.athleteDev: Use NHE blocks to build eccentric hamstring strength and balance in sprinters. Rope assistance in early sessions helped athletes learn controlled full-range execution, and strength tested two weeks after the block captured the largest gains.
paper.rtp: The study measured strength and muscle balance in healthy sprinters and did not test injured athletes or return-to-sport criteria. It cannot be used to decide when an athlete is ready to return after a hamstring injury.

records.sourceFile: Video Analysis of Anterior Cruciate                                Ligament Tears in Professional American    Football               Athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Johnston JT, Mandelbaum BR, Schub D, Rodeo SA, Matava MJ, Silvers HJ, et al. Video Analysis of Anterior Cruciate Ligament Tears in Professional American Football Athletes. Am J Sports Med. 2018.
paper.abstract: Video analysis of 69 NFL ACL injuries from the 2013-2016 seasons, with most injuries occurring without contact and a dynamic valgus knee position.
paper.tldr: Most ACL tears in these NFL players happened without contact, usually while pivoting or cutting. This points to noncontact mechanisms as a target for injury prevention work.
paper.methods: Retrospective case series of NFL players with ACL injuries from three seasons, found through public online databases and media. Two reviewers independently viewed the video of each injury to record mechanism, lower limb position and football activity.
paper.findings: Of 69 injuries with video, 50 (72.5%) were noncontact. Offensive linemen had a noncontact mechanism in 3 of 12 injuries (25%). For noncontact injuries, the most common activity was pivoting or cutting (30 of 50), and the injured limb most often showed hip abduction and flexion with early knee flexion and abduction. Noncontact proportions were similar on natural grass (75%) and artificial turf (70%), but no exposure data were available to test associations.
paper.limitations: Retrospective and based on public video, so some injuries were not captured. Video cannot measure force, there was no comparison group, and without exposure data the authors could not say whether position, timing or surface relate to injury incidence or mechanism. The abstract gives 20% noncontact for offensive linemen while Table 4 and the results text give 25% (3 of 12); this record uses the table value.
paper.practicalImplications: In this NFL sample, most ACL tears were noncontact, so prevention planning for cutting and pivoting athletes should include noncontact mechanisms. Offensive linemen were the exception, so their contact-related risk may need separate attention.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: Cutting and pivoting were the most common activities in noncontact ACL tears, so technique work on knee and hip alignment during cuts is a reasonable focus for position-specific prevention. The paper does not test any training intervention.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: The study does not address rehabilitation or return-to-play decisions and should not be used to judge readiness after ACL reconstruction.

records.sourceFile: Video analysis of reported concussion events in the NFL.pdf

paper.citation: Lessley DJ, Kent RW, Funk JR, Sherwood CP, Cormier JM, Crandall JR, et al. Video Analysis of Reported Concussion Events in the National Football League During the 2015-2016 and 2016-2017 Seasons. Am J Sports Med. 2018.
paper.abstract: Video review of 458 NFL concussions reported in two seasons, with standardized definitions of the injury play, activity and helmet impact.
paper.tldr: NFL concussion causes have shifted, with more helmet-to-body and helmet-to-ground impacts and fewer helmet-to-helmet impacts than in earlier seasons. Tackling was the most common activity of concussed players.
paper.methods: All concussions reported to the league in the two seasons were reviewed with all available game video. Standardized terms defined the injury play, primary exposure, player activity, helmet impact location and impact source.
paper.findings: Cornerbacks sustained the most concussions, followed by wide receivers, linebackers and offensive linemen. Half of concussions (50%) occurred on passing plays, and 21% on punts or kickoffs. Tackling was the most common activity, and the side of the helmet was the most common impact location. Helmet-to-body (particularly shoulder) and helmet-to-ground impacts were more common, and helmet-to-helmet impacts less common, than in earlier seasons. The rear of the helmet was struck in 37% of helmet-to-ground impacts, and helmet-to-ground impacts made up a larger share of concussions on passing plays.
paper.limitations: Only reported concussions were included, and the injury play was identified in 83% of cases. Video does not show every impact, and there is no denominator of plays or exposures. The study was sponsored with NFL support, and a company owned by two authors receives NFL consulting fees, including for this study.
paper.practicalImplications: Concussion countermeasures should address ground and body impacts as well as helmet-to-helmet contact, as the authors suggest. Position patterns, such as cornerbacks and passing plays, may help target coaching review, but this descriptive study cannot show that they represent higher risk.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: Almost twice as many concussions occurred while tackling as while being tackled, mostly from contact with the ball carrier's body, which the authors suggest supports continued teaching of tackling technique that minimizes helmet impacts for the tackler. The study does not show that any coaching change reduces concussions.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: The study describes how concussions happen and does not evaluate return-to-play protocols or recovery times. It should not be used to set return-to-play timing.

records.sourceFile: Visuomotor strateiges for collision avoidance in athletes - Insights from virtual reality.pdf

paper.citation: Kiefer AW, Aitcheson-Huehn N, Armitano-Lago CN, MacPherson R, Willoughby D, Silva PL. Visuomotor strategies for collision avoidance in athletes: Insights from virtual reality. J Sci Med Sport. 2024.
paper.abstract: VR study of 39 athletes avoiding virtual defenders, where two head-scanning features were linked to whether collisions occurred.
paper.tldr: In a VR navigation task, a greater amount of head rotation went with avoiding virtual defenders (only with two defenders), while a more varied pattern of head movement went with collisions. This links scanning to collision avoidance but does not test injury outcomes.
paper.methods: Thirty-nine healthy collegiate club or varsity contact-sport athletes (14 female) completed 48 trials in VR, pursuing a virtual target while avoiding 2 to 5 virtual defenders. Head rotations were sampled at 72 Hz. Confirmatory factor analysis built a two-factor scanning model, and linear mixed models tested its link to collision outcomes.
paper.findings: The overall amount of head rotation (factor 1) was higher in avoidance interactions, but only in the two-defender condition (p = .001). The temporal variability of head movement (factor 2) was higher during interactions that led to collision, regardless of condition (p = .01). The authors report that scanning features significantly differentiated successful from unsuccessful avoidance (p < .05).
paper.limitations: Small sample and a virtual task, with no fear of collision or real competition present. Head rotation was used as a proxy for scanning without eye tracking, collisions were few (108 versus 1237 non-collisions), and the outcome is collisions in VR, not injury. The authors note that the results need confirmation in sport.
paper.practicalImplications: Scanning behavior is associated with avoiding collisions in a VR task, so visual scanning may be worth including in collision-awareness training. Staff should not treat this as proof that scanning training reduces injury.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: Head scanning while navigating past opponents is a plausible focus for collision-avoidance practice, but more scanning helped only in the simplest condition and more varied head movement went with collisions, so 'scan more' is not a supported cue. The study has not tested whether training scanning improves on-field avoidance.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: The study uses healthy athletes and does not assess return to sport or rehabilitation. It cannot be used to judge readiness after a head or collision injury.

paper.citation: Clugston JR, Diemer K, Chrabaszcz SL, et al. What are the Protocols and Resources for Sport-Related Concussion Among Top National Collegiate Athletic Association Football Programs? A Cross-Sectional Survey of A5 Schools. Clin J Sport Med. 2024.
paper.abstract: This cross-sectional survey of NCAA Division 1 Autonomy Five football programs describes sport-related concussion protocols for the 2018 season, collected from athletic trainers and team physicians before a June 2019 NFL-NCAA football safety meeting. Of 46 responding programs, nearly all measured baseline balance, most used neurocognitive testing, and fewer than two-thirds assessed vestibular and/or ocular function at baseline. Prevention practices and the timing of post-concussion aerobic exercise varied widely across programs. The authors conclude that protocols are not standardized and that the findings are descriptive.
paper.tldr: Baseline balance and neurocognitive testing are near-universal among top collegiate football programs, but vestibular and ocular testing, prevention practices and the timing of post-concussion exercise vary widely. Use these figures to benchmark a local protocol, not as proof that any one approach works.
paper.methods: Electronic surveys with 16 concussion-related questions were sent to athletic trainers and team physicians at the 65 A5 football programs; 46 programs responded, with one aggregate response allowed per institution. Responses covered baseline assessment, prevention and management for the 2018 season, and were analyzed with descriptive statistics only.
paper.findings: Baseline postural stability/balance was assessed by 98% of programs and computerized neurocognitive testing by 87%, while 61% assessed vestibular and/or ocular function. For prevention (multiple answers allowed, 51 responses), 49% of responses recommended a measure: 24% omega-3 supplements, 22% external helmet padding and 4% cervical compression collars. After concussion, 26% began light aerobic exercise the day after if symptoms were stable, 24% waited 48 hours, 11% waited until the athlete was asymptomatic, 4% waited until baseline, and 35% decided case by case.
paper.limitations: The survey reflects the 2018 season and not current practice, and the 46 responding programs may not represent all A5 schools. Response rates varied by question (45% to 71%), respondent demographics were unavailable, and multi-select questions make cross-program comparison harder. The abstract says most institutions started light aerobic exercise within 48 hours, but the results show 50% did (26% on day 1 plus 24% at 48 hours) and the discussion says only half did; the results figures are used here.
paper.practicalImplications: Programs can compare their baseline battery with these A5 figures, and the authors advise broader vestibular and ocular baseline testing, which 39% of programs did not perform. The authors state the evidence is insufficient to endorse omega-3 supplementation and does not show that cervical compression collars reduce concussion risk; for external helmet padding they call the evidence limited but suggest collegiate teams consider the Guardian Cap while research continues.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: This is not a performance study. The transferable point is the baseline screening menu: balance and neurocognitive tests are common, while vestibular and ocular screens are used by about 61% of programs, and these are concussion baselines rather than training measures.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: The study describes post-concussion aerobic exercise timing but does not test outcomes, so it cannot show which timing returns athletes to play safely or sooner. It can support checking that a local protocol is written down and matches the consensus timing the authors cite (subthreshold activity on day 1 and controlled aerobic exercise within 2 days).
